Use Artificial Intelligence as a Sparring Partner, Not as the Author Finish With a Question or an Invitation A Small Start Writing Product Management Software Development UX Writing Tips What I Wish I Had Known Before I Started Writing About Product Management Anika Wübben 4 min read · Oct 25, 2026 -- Listen Share Eight lessons from turning a frustration into articles that people answer. When I started writing, I did not have an audience. I had a frustration. For years I had noticed a gap between what product management could be and what it usually is, and I could not stop thinking about it. Writing was the only way to find out whether it made sense to anyone but me. What I learned is that writing is the same craft as the job: know the problem, know who it is for, and finish the thinking before you hand it over. Most Product Managers already do that every day. What they rarely do is publish. Here is what I would tell myself at the start. The moment it clicked for me was a short message from a developer. He wrote that the gap I describe is something he feels a lot. Not "interesting article." Not "good points." He felt it. I had not told him anything new. I had put words on something he already knew and could not name. Everything below is about how to write toward that reaction. 1. Start With a Gap, Not a Topic "Roadmaps" is a topic. "Why teams keep missing roadmaps they estimated carefully" is a gap. A gap is the distance between how something works and how it could work, and you have probably felt one in your own team. Topics produce summaries. Gaps produce articles with a point of view. If you cannot name the gap in one sentence, you are not ready to write. 2. Write for One Reader Decide who you want to change something. Not who might read it, but who could act on it. A designer can recognize a problem. A person in senior management can decide whether the organization keeps tolerating it. Once you know your reader, many decisions get easier: which terms to explain, which examples to use, and what the last paragraph should ask for. 3. Use Your Own Mistakes Generic advice is everywhere. What nobody else has is your specific experience: the requirement you wrote that cost a team two weeks, the decision you got wrong, the standard you built afterward. Readers can tell the difference between someone theorizing and someone who has sat across the table from the people affected. Lived experience is the only thing a machine cannot copy, so it is also your strongest asset. 4. Be Able to Say Where a Number Comes From A statistic makes an argument feel solid, and an unchecked statistic can sink the whole piece. Before you publish, trace every figure to its original source and read the sentence around it. Does it say what you are about to claim? Is it a survey of opinions, or a measurement? Was the sample small? Say so in the text. A study with 54 participants is a signal, not a verdict, and readers trust you more when you tell them that. 5. Carry One Thesis Through Every Section Write your main idea as one sentence. Then test every section against it. If a section only sits next to the thesis without leading to it, either add the missing link or cut it. I check this by asking one question per section: why does this belong here, and what sentence connects it to the point? The answer is often a missing bridge, and one added sentence fixes it. 6. Explain Your Terms Every field has words that feel obvious inside it. Product Increment is a good example: clear to someone certified in a framework, opaque to everyone else. If your reader has to stop and decode a term, you have lost them for a moment, and moments add up. Use plain language first. If a term matters, introduce it once, on purpose, with a sentence of context. 7. Keep the Tone Respectful Sharp opinions work. Bitter ones do not. Watch for sentences that dismiss a group, call a debate lazy, or imply that the reader is part of the problem. Say the same thing without the edge. If you disagree with how people work, describe what you see and what it costs. The reader will draw the conclusion, and they will stay for the rest of the article. 8. Use Artificial Intelligence as a Sparring Partner, Not as the Author Think first. Write down your own answer, even a rough one. Then use the tool to find the gap you missed, to challenge a weak argument, or to tighten a clumsy paragraph. If the tool writes the thinking for you, the article loses the one thing that made it yours, and you lose the practice that makes you better at the job. Finish With a Question or an Invitation End on something the reader can act on: a question that makes them look at their own team, or an invitation to talk. The comments that follow are where most of the learning happens. Every real reaction tells you whether the gap you named is shared. A Small Start Pick one gap you have personally experienced. Write it as one sentence. Name the one person who could act on it. Then write the shortest article that gets that person to think differently. What is the gap you keep noticing in your own work, and who needs to read about it?
